claims.text: A thin ordered NiAl interlayer has the B2 phase.
Adding a thin NiAl interlayer between HEA layers enables interface coherency to be tuned.
Tuning coherency with a NiAl interlayer causes a transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep.
The initial HEA-only multilayers possess inherent lattice distortions.
The initial HEA-only multilayers have relatively uncontrolled interface coherency.
Controlled deposition of a thin NiAl layer creates coherent interfaces with adjacent HEA layers.
High-temperature creep testing above approximately 700 °C is an applicable test regime for HEAs.
Under the proposed applied stresses, long-range diffusion and dislocation motion are both active.
The ordered B2 NiAl interlayer acts as a structural mediator between diffusion-controlled and dislocation-controlled creep regimes.
A coherent NiAl interlayer modifies the local atomic structure at the HEA interface.
The coherent NiAl interlayer lowers the interfacial diffusion barrier.
Lowering the interfacial diffusion barrier promotes diffusion-mediated creep.
The coherent NiAl interlayer acts as a barrier to dislocation nucleation.
NiAl layer thickness and processing parameters can tune interface coherency.
NiAl-containing HEA multilayers will exhibit a measurable change from predominantly diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
HEA multilayers without NiAl are expected to lack a clearly defined creep-mechanism transition because their interface coherency is uncontrolled.
The beneficial effect occurs only within an optimal range of NiAl thickness and coherency.
An excessively thick NiAl layer or a poorly coherent interface may degrade mechanical performance or fail to mediate the proposed creep transition.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says that the NiAl interlayer inhibits dislocation nucleation, while the hypothesis and predicted outcome say it enables a transition toward dislocation-mediated creep. No condition-dependent explanation reconciles inhibition of dislocation nucleation with dominance of dislocation-mediated deformation.
